content: The outcomes of 328 cases in China were analyzed and published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2009. This study provided insights into the clinical effectiveness of circumcision techniques. Li HN, Xu J, and Qu LM conducted a comparative study between Shang Ring circumcision and conventional surgical procedures, focusing on clinical effectiveness. Their findings were published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2010. Peng YF, Yang BH, Jia C, and Jiang J reported on standardized male circumcision using the Shang Ring, highlighting its ability to reduce postoperative complications. Their study, involving 351 cases, was published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2010. Cheng Y, Yan Z, Su X, Fang H, Hu J, Wu K, and colleagues performed a clinical comparative study of Shang Ring circumcision versus conventional circumcision. Their findings were published in the Chinese Journal of Urology in 2011. Wang R, Chen WJ, Shi WH, and Xue YF conducted a comparative study of Shang Ring, sleeve, and conventional circumcision techniques for redundant prepuce and phimosis. Their analysis of 918 cases was published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2013. Liu C, Liu XJ, Mu JG, Liu D, Ren YS, and Zhang CL described a novel Shang Ring circumcision technique involving transverse incision and pull-up of the interior foreskin board for short frenulum. Their findings were published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2014. Xie ST, Chen GY, Wei QH, Liu XT, Jiao L, and Tang Y analyzed the outcomes of outward versus inward placement of the Shang Ring for phimosis and redundant prepuce in adult men. Their study of 527 cases was published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2014. Tang XH, Zhang P, Ding H, Zhao JH, Tang LL, and Fang Q compared Shang Ring scissor circumcision with electrotome circumcision for redundant prepuce. Their findings were published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2016. Wang SX, Zhang ZB, Yang SF, Yang EM, Pan DS, Xie XQ, and colleagues compared the Shang Ring with a disposable circumcision suture device for treating phimosis or redundant prepuce. Their study was published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2016. Yang BH, Jia C, Liu T, and Peng YF introduced a novel no-flip Shang Ring circumcision technique for adult males, analyzing 528 cases. Their findings were published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2014. Lei JH, Liu LR, Lu X, Cheng SH, Cai YC, Chen YJ, and colleagues analyzed the outcomes of circumcision using the no-flip Shang Ring technique in 168 adult males. Their study was published in the National Journal of Andrology in 2014. A GRADE evidence profile assessed whether elastic collar compression devices could serve as an alternative to surgery for circumcision in men aged 15–49 years for HIV prevention. The analysis, led by Tim Farley, evaluated safety, acceptability, and effectiveness. The findings suggested that further research is unlikely to change the estimates of outcomes such as eligibility, successful circumcision, procedure time, and acceptability. Studies on the PrePex device for non-surgical male circumcision in resource-limited settings demonstrated its safety, efficacy, and acceptability. These studies, conducted in countries like Rwanda, Uganda, Zimbabwe, and South Africa, highlighted outcomes such as adverse events, procedure times, pain, healing time, and cosmetic satisfaction. The PrePex device was found to be a viable alternative to surgical circumcision in many cases. The Unicirc device, a novel disposable circumcision instrument, was evaluated in South Africa. Studies demonstrated its rapid, minimally invasive nature and high levels of safety and satisfaction among adult males. The device was tested in multiple cohorts, with outcomes including adverse events, procedure times, wound healing, and cosmetic results. Overall, device-based methods of circumcision, such as the Shang Ring, PrePex, and Unicirc, have shown comparable efficacy to conventional surgical techniques. These devices offer advantages such as reduced procedure times and lower rates of adverse events when performed by trained healthcare workers. However, further research is needed to optimize their use, particularly in younger age groups and resource-limited settings.
